content.title: Start gathering evidence the offering achieves its outcome
content.finding: No evidence has been gathered on whether the product or service actually achieves the outcome customers need when they use it for its core purpose.
content.consequence: The business doesn't yet know whether what it delivers actually works for its intended purpose — everything else about the offering (pricing, positioning, expansion) is being built on an unconfirmed foundation.
content.action: Start gathering anecdotal impressions from customers or early users about whether the offering helps them achieve the outcome they need — informal feedback is enough to start.
content.avoid: Assuming it works because it was built to the specification. A specification being met is not the same as the customer's outcome being achieved.
content.action_evidence: Anecdotal impressions from customers or users suggest the offering helps, even without systematic observation yet.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: do anecdotal impressions suggest it helps, even without anything measured systematically? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Confirm the outcome through observation or structured feedback
content.finding: Anecdotal impressions suggest the offering helps, but nothing has been observed or measured systematically to confirm it.
content.consequence: The business is currently relying on scattered impressions rather than anything it could point to with confidence if asked whether the offering actually works.
content.action: Directly observe customers using the offering, or gather structured feedback, specifically to confirm the outcome is achieved in typical cases.
content.avoid: Relying on a single, especially enthusiastic customer's account as if it represented the typical case.
content.action_evidence: Direct observation or structured feedback confirms the outcome is achieved in typical use cases.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does direct observation or structured feedback confirm the outcome is achieved in typical cases? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Confirm the outcome across a real range of customers and use cases
content.finding: The outcome is confirmed in typical cases, but not yet across the fuller range of customers and use cases the business actually serves.
content.consequence: What's confirmed to work for a typical customer may not hold for customers at the edges of who the business serves — the business doesn't yet know where its offering's real limits are.
content.action: Extend the confirmation beyond typical or best-case customers to a genuine range of use cases, including ones that are more demanding or less standard.
content.avoid: Testing only with the easiest, most cooperative customers and calling that a range. The range needs to include the harder cases, not just more of the easy ones.
content.action_evidence: The outcome has been confirmed across a range of customers and use cases, not only typical or best-case ones.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the outcome confirmed across a range of customers and use cases, not only typical ones? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Start tracking failures, even informally
content.finding: Reliability isn't tracked, or failures are the norm rather than the exception.
content.consequence: The business doesn't know how often what it delivers fails the customer — without tracking, there's no way to tell if things are improving, worsening, or staying the same.
content.action: Start informally tracking defects, failures, or errors that affect customers, even without a systematic process yet.
content.avoid: Only noting failures that generate a customer complaint. Many failures go unreported — informal tracking still needs to actively look, not just wait for complaints.
content.action_evidence: Failures affecting customers are being noted, even informally.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is reliability tracked informally, even if recurring issues still require individual fixes? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Catch and resolve most failures with more consistency
content.finding: Reliability is tracked informally, but recurring issues still require individual fixes each time they occur.
content.consequence: The business is spending effort fixing the same kinds of problems repeatedly, rather than catching and resolving them systematically before they recur.
content.action: Bring more consistency to tracking, so most instances of failure are caught and resolved, even if not yet systematically prevented from recurring.
content.avoid: Fixing each instance without ever asking whether it's the same underlying issue recurring. That keeps the fixing effort constant instead of declining.
content.action_evidence: Most instances of failure are being caught and resolved with reasonable consistency.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is reliability tracked with some consistency, with most instances caught and resolved? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Make failures the exception through systematic tracking
content.finding: Reliability is tracked with some consistency and most failures are caught, but they aren't yet systematically prevented — failures are still a regular occurrence, not an exception.
content.consequence: The business is still catching problems after the fact rather than having reduced how often they happen — reactive, not yet in control of its own reliability.
content.action: Move to systematic tracking, and use it to address root causes so that failures become the exception rather than a recurring pattern.
content.avoid: Adding more monitoring without acting on what it reveals. Tracking that doesn't change the underlying failure rate isn't yet systematic in the way this item requires.
content.action_evidence: Reliability is tracked systematically, and failures are demonstrably the exception rather than a recurring pattern.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is reliability tracked systematically, with failures the exception rather than the norm? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Close the gap forcing the most disruptive workaround
content.finding: Significant gaps in the offering force customers to rely on manual workarounds or other providers for essential parts of their core need.
content.consequence: Customers currently have to patch together what the business doesn't fully deliver — a real friction that makes the offering less valuable, and an opening for a more complete competitor.
content.action: Identify the most significant gap forcing a workaround, and close enough of it that customers manage the remaining gaps rather than routing around the business entirely for essential parts of the need.
content.avoid: Adding unrelated new features instead of closing the specific gaps forcing workarounds. Breadth doesn't help if the core need still isn't fully covered.
content.action_evidence: The most significant workaround-forcing gap has been closed, even if smaller gaps remain and customers still raise them.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: do gaps exist that customers manage, having raised them as real friction, rather than gaps forcing workarounds? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Cover the core need fully, leaving only adjacent gaps
content.finding: Some gaps exist in the offering; customers manage them, but have raised them as real friction.
content.consequence: Customers are currently tolerating gaps rather than being fully served — tolerance can run out, especially if an alternative appears that doesn't have the same gaps.
content.action: Close the gaps affecting the customer's core need specifically, even if gaps in adjacent or secondary needs remain for now.
content.avoid: Prioritizing gaps by how easy they are to fix rather than by whether they affect the customer's actual core need.
content.action_evidence: The core need is now covered; any remaining known gaps concern adjacent or secondary needs, not the core one.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the core need covered, with known gaps concerning only adjacent or secondary needs? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Get customers to confirm completeness, not just the business's own view
content.finding: The core need is covered, with known gaps limited to adjacent or secondary needs — solid, but this has been assessed internally rather than confirmed by customers.
content.consequence: The business's own view that the core need is fully covered hasn't yet been checked against what customers actually experience — an internal assumption can miss gaps customers see but haven't flagged as strongly.
content.action: Confirm directly with customers that the core need is covered with no material gaps, rather than relying on the business's own internal assessment.
content.avoid: Asking customers a general satisfaction question and treating a positive answer as confirmation of completeness. Ask specifically about gaps in the core need.
content.action_evidence: Customer feedback specifically confirms the core need is covered with no material gaps.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the core need covered with no material gaps, confirmed by customer feedback rather than internal assumption? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Start collecting feedback instead of waiting for complaints
content.finding: There is no systematic collection of feedback on how the product or service performs — issues surface only if a customer happens to complain.
content.consequence: The business is currently blind to problems customers don't bother to report — for every complaint received, there may be several unreported issues quietly affecting satisfaction or retention.
content.action: Start collecting feedback on how the offering performs, even informally and inconsistently, rather than waiting for complaints.
content.avoid: Treating the absence of complaints as the absence of problems. Most dissatisfied customers don't complain — they just leave.
content.action_evidence: Feedback is being collected informally, even without a consistent process yet.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is feedback collected informally and inconsistently, even without a clear process for acting on it? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Make sure feedback actually leads to changes
content.finding: Feedback is collected informally and inconsistently, with no clear process for acting on what's collected.
content.consequence: Feedback is currently being gathered without reliably being used — insight is being collected and then not consistently turned into anything.
content.action: Bring more consistency to collection, and make sure at least some of what's collected visibly leads to changes in the offering.
content.avoid: Collecting more feedback without changing whether or how it gets acted on. More input doesn't help if the same share of it gets ignored.
content.action_evidence: Feedback is collected with reasonable consistency, and some of it visibly leads to changes.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is feedback collected with some consistency, with some of it visibly leading to changes? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Establish a defined feedback channel with a consistent response pattern
content.finding: Feedback is collected with some consistency and some of it leads to changes, but there's no defined channel or process behind it — it's still somewhat ad hoc.
content.consequence: Without a defined channel, feedback collection depends on remembering to ask rather than being a reliable, repeatable part of how the business runs.
content.action: Establish a defined channel or process for collecting feedback, and act on it consistently enough that a real pattern of response is visible.
content.avoid: Setting up a feedback channel that collects input but isn't actually reviewed on any regular basis. The process needs to include acting on it, not just gathering it.
content.action_evidence: A defined feedback channel or process exists, with a consistent pattern of acting on what it surfaces.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is feedback collected through a defined channel or process, with a consistent pattern of acting on it? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Standardize the first parts of delivery
content.finding: Every delivery requires substantial bespoke, non-repeatable effort — the founder or a specialist is required each time.
content.consequence: Delivery currently can't scale beyond whoever is doing the bespoke work — growth in demand translates directly into more strain on that same person, rather than being absorbable.
content.action: Identify which parts of delivery could be made repeatable, and start standardizing at least some of them, even if delivery still depends heavily on specific individuals overall.
content.avoid: Documenting the process the founder already follows without actually simplifying or standardizing it. Writing down bespoke work doesn't make it repeatable.
content.action_evidence: Some parts of delivery are now repeatable, even though delivery overall still depends heavily on specific individuals or ad hoc effort.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are some parts of delivery repeatable, even if it still depends heavily on specific individuals? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Systematize core delivery so exceptions are the minority
content.finding: Some parts of delivery are repeatable, but it still depends heavily on specific individuals or ad hoc effort overall.
content.consequence: Delivery capacity is currently tied to particular people's availability and effort rather than to a process the business could hand to someone else or scale.
content.action: Systematize core delivery — document it, template it, or productize it — so exceptions requiring bespoke work become the minority of what delivery involves, not the majority.
content.avoid: Systematizing the easy, low-value parts of delivery while leaving the core of what customers actually pay for as bespoke as ever.
content.action_evidence: Core delivery is documented, templated, or productized, even if exceptions still require significant bespoke work.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is core delivery systematised, even if exceptions still require significant bespoke work? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Make bespoke handling the exception, not the routine
content.finding: Core delivery is systematised, but bespoke handling is still common rather than the exception — a meaningful share of delivery still falls outside the standard process.
content.consequence: The business has a standard process, but relies on it inconsistently — much of delivery is still effectively being done the old, bespoke way.
content.action: Extend the standard process to cover more of what delivery actually involves, so bespoke handling becomes the exception rather than a routine occurrence.
content.avoid: Treating the existence of a documented process as sufficient, without checking how much of actual delivery goes through it versus around it.
content.action_evidence: Most delivery now goes through the standard process, with bespoke handling limited to genuine exceptions.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is bespoke handling the exception, with most delivery going through the standard process? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.
